Anatomy-03.question: ১) Which layer of meninges directs contacts neural tissue?
Anatomy-03.exp:
The pia mater is the innermost meningeal layer and is firmly adherent to the surface of the brain and spinal cord, closely following all the gyri, sulci, and fissures. It is a thin, highly vascular membrane that directly contacts the neural tissue and supports the blood vessels supplying the central nervous system. In contrast, the dura mater is the tough outermost meningeal layer, while the arachnoid mater is the middle avascular membrane separated from the pia by the subarachnoid space, which contains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Therefore, the pia mater is the only meningeal layer that directly contacts neural tissue.

Exam pearl:

  • Dura mater → Outermost, tough protective layer.

  • Arachnoid mater → Middle layer; subarachnoid space contains CSF.

  • Pia mater → Innermost, directly adherent to the brain and spinal cord.

Anatomy-03.question: ২) Unipolar neuron
৩) Basal nuclei excludes
Anatomy-03.exp:
The basal nuclei (basal ganglia) are collections of gray matter within the cerebral hemispheres involved in the regulation of voluntary movement. They include the corpus striatum (caudate nucleus and lentiform nucleus), claustrum, and amygdaloid nucleus in the classical anatomical classification. The emboliform nucleus, however, is not a basal nucleus; it is one of the deep cerebellar nuclei (along with the dentate, globose, and fastigial nuclei) and is involved in coordination of movement. Therefore, emboliform is excluded from the basal nuclei.

Exam pearl:

  • Basal nuclei (classical anatomy): Corpus striatum, claustrum, amygdaloid nucleus.

  • Deep cerebellar nuclei: Dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial.

  • Clinical: Basal ganglia lesions cause movement disorders (e.g., Parkinson disease, Huntington disease).

৩১) Most superficial layer of cerebram
Anatomy-03.exp:
The most superficial layer of the cerebral cortex is the molecular layer (Layer I). It lies immediately beneath the pia mater and contains relatively few neuronal cell bodies. Instead, it is composed mainly of nerve fibers (axons and dendrites) and scattered horizontal cells of Cajal, serving as an important site for synaptic connections. The remaining cortical layers, from superficial to deep, are external granular (II), external pyramidal (III), internal granular (IV), internal pyramidal (V), and multiform/polymorphic (VI).

Exam pearl:
The six layers of the cerebral cortex (superficial → deep) are:

  1. Molecular (I)

  2. External granular (II)

  3. External pyramidal (III)

  4. Internal granular (IV)

  5. Internal pyramidal (V)

  6. Multiform/Polymorphic (VI)

Anatomy-03.question: ৩২) Anosmia is a disorder of which sensation?
Anatomy-03.exp:
Anosmia is the complete loss of the sense of smell (olfaction). It commonly results from disorders affecting the olfactory epithelium, olfactory nerve (CN I), olfactory bulb, or central olfactory pathways. Common causes include upper respiratory viral infections, nasal obstruction, head trauma (causing shearing of olfactory nerve filaments at the cribriform plate), neurodegenerative diseases, and tumors. Anosmia often leads to a diminished perception of flavor, which may be mistaken for loss of taste, although the primary deficit is olfactory rather than gustatory.

Exam pearl:

  • Anosmia → Loss of smell (CN I)

  • Ageusia → Loss of taste

  • Anacusis → Complete hearing loss

  • Amaurosis → Loss of vision

Anatomy-03.question: ৩৩) Which type of papillae contains most taste bud
Anatomy-03.exp:
Circumvallate (vallate) papillae contain the greatest number of taste buds per papilla. There are 8–12 large circumvallate papillae arranged in a V-shaped row just anterior to the sulcus terminalis. Their lateral walls contain numerous taste buds, and they are associated with the von Ebner serous glands, which help wash away tastants. Fungiform papillae contain a few taste buds on their upper surface, foliate papillae have taste buds mainly in children and are less developed in adults, and filiform papillae are the most numerous but contain no taste buds, serving a mechanical function.

Exam pearl:

  • Filiform → Most numerous, no taste buds

  • Fungiform → Few taste buds

  • Foliate → Taste buds on lateral folds (more prominent in children)

  • Circumvallate (Vallate) → Largest number of taste buds per papilla; supplied mainly by CN IX (Glossopharyngeal nerve).

Anatomy-03.question: ৩৪) Signs of cerebellar lesion excludes
৩৫) Typical sweat gland are of... variety
Anatomy-03.exp:
The typical sweat glands of the body are eccrine sweat glands, and their mode of secretion is merocrine (exocytosis without loss of cytoplasm). Since the question asks for the variety of the sweat gland based on its secretory mechanism, the single best answer is merocrine. Apocrine glands are found mainly in the axilla, areola, and perineum and become active after puberty. Holocrine secretion is characteristic of sebaceous glands, where the entire cell disintegrates to release its contents.

Note: This MCQ is slightly ambiguous because "typical sweat gland" may refer to either the type of gland (eccrine) or the mode of secretion (merocrine). Based on the wording "are of... variety," merocrine is the best answer.

Exam pearl:

  • Eccrine sweat gland → Merocrine secretion, thermoregulation, distributed over most of the body.

  • Apocrine sweat gland → Axilla, areola, perineum; opens into hair follicles.

  • Sebaceous gland → Holocrine secretion.

Anatomy-03.question: ৩৬) Layers of hair follicle excludes
Anatomy-03.exp:
The hair shaft consists of three concentric layers: the cuticle (outer protective layer), cortex (middle layer containing keratin and pigment), and medulla (central core, usually present in thick hairs). Zonule is not a layer of the hair or hair follicle; it commonly refers to the ciliary zonule (suspensory ligament of the lens) in the eye. Therefore, among the given options, zonule is correctly excluded.

Note: The question is slightly flawed. The listed structures (cuticle, cortex, medulla) are layers of the hair shaft, not the hair follicle. Histologically, the hair follicle consists of the inner root sheath, outer root sheath, glassy membrane, and connective tissue sheath. However, in standard anatomy MCQs, the intended answer is Zonule.

Exam pearl:

  • Hair shaft layers: Cuticle → Cortex → Medulla

  • Hair follicle layers: Inner root sheath, Outer root sheath, Glassy membrane, Connective tissue sheath.

Anatomy-03.question: ৩৭) Predominant cell type of epidermis
Anatomy-03.exp:
Keratinocytes are the predominant cell type of the epidermis, accounting for approximately 90–95% of all epidermal cells. They originate from the stratum basale and migrate toward the surface, undergoing keratinization to form the protective barrier of the skin. This barrier prevents water loss and protects against physical, chemical, and microbial injury. In contrast, melanocytes produce melanin pigment, Langerhans cells function as antigen-presenting immune cells, and Merkel cells are mechanoreceptors involved in light touch sensation. Therefore, keratinocyte is the single best answer.

Exam pearl:

  • Keratinocytes → 90–95% of epidermal cells; produce keratin.

  • Melanocytes → Melanin production (stratum basale).

  • Langerhans cells → Antigen-presenting cells (stratum spinosum).

  • Merkel cells → Touch receptors (stratum basale).

Anatomy-03.question: ৩৮) The most abundant type of cerebral cortical neurons are the
Anatomy-03.exp:
Pyramidal cells are the most abundant neurons in the cerebral cortex, comprising approximately 70–80% of cortical neurons. They are excitatory (glutamatergic) projection neurons and are found predominantly in layers III and V of the cerebral cortex. Their axons form association, commissural, and corticospinal pathways. In contrast, stellate (granule) cells are mainly local interneurons, Purkinje cells are the principal neurons of the cerebellar cortex, and fusiform (multiform) cells are found mainly in the deepest cortical layer (layer VI) and are less numerous.

Exam pearl:

  • Pyramidal cells → Most abundant cerebral cortical neurons; excitatory, glutamatergic.

  • Purkinje cells → Cerebellar cortex; only output neurons of the cerebellar cortex; inhibitory (GABAergic).

  • Stellate cells → Local interneurons, especially prominent in layer IV.

  • Fusiform cells → Predominantly located in layer VI (multiform layer).

Anatomy-03.question: ৩৯) Neuroglia in PNS
৪০) The substance of the tongue is made up chiefly of
Anatomy-03.exp:
The tongue is composed predominantly of skeletal (striated) muscle arranged in interlacing bundles. These muscles are divided into intrinsic muscles, which alter the shape of the tongue, and extrinsic muscles, which change its position. The skeletal muscles are covered by a mucous membrane containing connective tissue, glands, and taste buds. Smooth muscle is not a component of the tongue's substance, while connective tissue and epithelium provide support and surface covering but do not constitute the chief bulk of the organ. Therefore, skeletal muscle is the single best answer.

Exam pearl:

  • Tongue substance → Skeletal muscle

  • Intrinsic muscles → Change the shape of the tongue.

  • Extrinsic muscles → Change the position of the tongue.

  • Motor supply: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) to all tongue muscles except palatoglossus, which is supplied by the vagus nerve (CN X).

Anatomy-03.question: ৪১) Most numerous papillae of tongue
Anatomy-03.exp:
Filiform papillae are the most numerous papillae on the dorsum of the tongue. They are slender, conical projections covered by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and serve a mechanical function, helping to grip and manipulate food. Unlike the other lingual papillae, filiform papillae do not contain taste buds. In contrast, fungiform, foliate, and circumvallate papillae contain taste buds and are involved in gustation. Therefore, the single best answer is filiform papillae.

Exam pearl:

  • Filiform → Most numerous, no taste buds, mechanical function.

  • Fungiform → Scattered among filiform papillae; contain taste buds.

  • Circumvallate → 8–12 large papillae arranged in a V-shape; contain the highest number of taste buds per papilla.

  • Foliate → Located on the lateral border of the tongue; taste buds are more prominent in children.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪২) Sclerocorneal junction is called
Anatomy-03.exp:
The sclerocorneal junction is known as the limbus (corneal limbus). It is the transitional zone between the transparent cornea and the opaque sclera. The limbus contains important structures such as the trabecular meshwork and the canal of Schlemm, which facilitate the drainage of aqueous humor and help maintain normal intraocular pressure. It also contains limbal stem cells, which are essential for regeneration of the corneal epithelium. The other options are unrelated: cristae are anatomical ridges, synapse is a neuronal junction, and nexus refers to a gap junction.

Exam pearl:

  • Sclerocorneal junction = Limbus

  • Canal of Schlemm and trabecular meshwork are located at the limbus.

  • Obstruction of aqueous humor drainage at this site contributes to open-angle glaucoma.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪৩) The cells of the epithelium are
Anatomy-03.exp:
This MCQ is incomplete/ambiguous because it does not specify which epithelium or organ is being referred to. Different organs have different epithelial cell types. In many anatomy MCQs, when the stem simply states "The cells of the epithelium are...", it commonly refers to the corneal epithelium or alveolar epithelium, where the cells are stratified squamous non-keratinized (cornea) or simple squamous (alveoli). Therefore, squamous is the best available answer.

Note: The question is flawed due to the lack of context. The correct epithelial type depends entirely on the tissue or organ being discussed.

Exam pearl:

  • Simple squamous epithelium → Alveoli, endothelium, mesothelium.

  • Stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium → Cornea, oral cavity, esophagus.

  • Simple cuboidal epithelium → Kidney tubules, thyroid follicles.

  • Simple columnar epithelium → Stomach, intestine.

  • Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium → Most of the respiratory tract.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪৪) The middle ear is placed within which bone?
Anatomy-03.exp:
The middle ear (tympanic cavity) is located within the petrous part of the temporal bone. It is an air-filled cavity containing the three auditory ossicles—malleus, incus, and stapes—which transmit sound vibrations from the tympanic membrane to the inner ear. The middle ear communicates anteriorly with the nasopharynx through the auditory (Eustachian) tube and posteriorly with the mastoid air cells via the aditus to the mastoid antrum. The frontal, parietal, and occipital bones do not house the middle ear.

Exam pearl:

  • Middle ear → Petrous part of the temporal bone

  • Contents: Malleus, Incus, Stapes

  • Communications: Eustachian tube (nasopharynx) and mastoid air cells

  • Inner ear (cochlea and vestibular apparatus) is also located within the petrous temporal bone.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪৫) Parts of the bony labyrinth excludes
Anatomy-03.exp:
The bony labyrinth is a system of cavities within the petrous part of the temporal bone and consists of three main parts: the vestibule, three semicircular canals, and the bony cochlea. It encloses the membranous labyrinth and is filled with perilymph. The saccule is not part of the bony labyrinth; it is a component of the membranous labyrinth located within the vestibule and contains sensory receptors for linear acceleration and head position. Therefore, saccule is correctly excluded.

Exam pearl:

  • Bony labyrinth → Vestibule + Semicircular canals + Bony cochlea (contains perilymph)

  • Membranous labyrinth → Utricle, Saccule, Semicircular ducts, Cochlear duct (contains endolymph)

Anatomy-03.question: ৪৬) The sensory organ of hearing is situated on
Anatomy-03.exp:
The organ of Corti, the sensory organ of hearing, is situated on the basilar membrane within the cochlear duct (scala media). It contains inner and outer hair cells, which convert sound vibrations into nerve impulses. The tectorial membrane lies over the hair cells; deflection of the stereocilia against this membrane during vibration generates receptor potentials, but the organ of Corti itself rests on the basilar membrane. The vestibular (Reissner's) membrane separates the scala vestibuli from the cochlear duct and is not the site of the hearing receptor. Therefore, the single best answer is basilar membrane.

Exam pearl:

  • Organ of Corti → Located on the basilar membrane

  • Tectorial membrane → Overlies the hair cells

  • Basilar membrane vibration determines sound frequency:

    • Base → High-frequency sounds

    • Apex → Low-frequency sounds

Anatomy-03.question: ৪৭) Which lines ventricular system?
Anatomy-03.exp:
Ependymal cells are ciliated neuroglial cells that line the ventricular system of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord. They form the epithelial lining of these cavities and help circulate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) through the coordinated beating of their cilia. Specialized ependymal cells in the choroid plexus are involved in CSF production. In contrast, astrocytes provide structural and metabolic support and contribute to the blood–brain barrier, oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons, and microglia are the resident phagocytic immune cells of the CNS.

Exam pearl:

  • Ependymal cells → Line brain ventricles and central canal; involved in CSF circulation and CSF production (choroid plexus).

  • Astrocytes → Blood–brain barrier, support.

  • Oligodendrocytes → CNS myelination.

  • Microglia → CNS macrophages/phagocytes.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪৮) The processes of astrocytes are united to those of other astrocytes through
Anatomy-03.exp:
Astrocytes are interconnected by gap junctions, which form a functional syncytium within the central nervous system. These junctions, composed of connexin proteins, allow the direct passage of ions and small molecules between adjacent astrocytes, facilitating potassium buffering, metabolic support, and intercellular calcium signaling. In contrast, tight junctions create impermeable barriers (e.g., between endothelial cells of the blood–brain barrier), desmosomes provide strong mechanical adhesion between cells, and hemidesmosomes anchor epithelial cells to the basement membrane. Therefore, gap junctions are the correct answer.

Exam pearl:

  • Astrocytes are connected by gap junctions.

  • Tight junctions → Blood–brain barrier, epithelial barriers.

  • Desmosomes → Cell-to-cell mechanical adhesion.

  • Hemidesmosomes → Cell-to-basement membrane attachment.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪৯) Which one is concerned with converting recent memory to long term memory?
Anatomy-03.exp:
The hippocampus is the principal structure responsible for consolidating recent (short-term) memory into long-term memory. It is located in the medial temporal lobe and is essential for the formation of new declarative memories (facts and events). Bilateral hippocampal damage results in anterograde amnesia, where the patient cannot form new long-term memories despite retaining previously established memories. The amygdala is primarily involved in emotional processing, especially fear and emotional memory, while the putamen and globus pallidus (pallidum) are components of the basal ganglia involved in motor control.

Exam pearl:

  • Hippocampus → Consolidation of short-term to long-term memory

  • Amygdala → Emotion, fear, emotional memory

  • Putamen + Globus pallidus → Motor control (basal ganglia)

  • Bilateral hippocampal lesions → Anterograde amnesia

Anatomy-03.question: ৫০) Actions of parasympathetic except
Anatomy-03.exp:
The parasympathetic nervous system is the "rest-and-digest" division of the autonomic nervous system. Its actions are aimed at conserving and restoring energy, slowing the heart rate, increasing gastrointestinal secretions, and enhancing gastrointestinal motility and peristalsis. Therefore, the statement "peristalsis is decreased" is incorrect and is the exception. A decrease in peristalsis is a sympathetic effect, which prepares the body for the "fight-or-flight" response by inhibiting digestive activity.

Exam pearl:
Parasympathetic effects:

  • Decreases heart rate

  • Increases peristalsis and GI secretions

  • Bronchoconstriction

  • Miosis (pupillary constriction)

  • Conserves and restores energy

Sympathetic effects: Increase heart rate, decrease peristalsis, bronchodilation, and mydriasis.
